html:
The Kazakh Khanate was a nomadic state of the Kazakh steppe, east of the Caspian and north of the Aral Sea, from about 1465 until the Russian Empire absorbed it in the first half of the 19th century.

It grew out of the break-up of the Golden Horde. Around 1465 two princes descended from Genghis Khan, Kerei and Janibek, led their followers away from the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr and set up on their own in the Zhetysu region. Their people became known as Kazakhs, roughly "free wanderers". While the Uzbeks moved south into the oasis cities, the Kazakhs kept the steppe and the herding life.

Its course:

  • Early 1500s: under Kasym Khan the Kazakhs held nearly the whole steppe. Many date the Kazakh state from his reign.
  • 1600s: power was split among three hordes, or zhuz: the Senior, Middle and Junior.
  • Late 1600s: Tauke Khan issued a law code and briefly held the hordes together. After his death in 1715 they drifted apart.
  • 1723: a great Dzungar invasion, remembered as the "Years of Great Disaster".
  • 1731 onward: the Junior Horde, then others, accepted Russian protection against the Dzungars.
  • Mid 1700s: Ablai Khan played Russia and the Qing against each other.

Russia built forts along the steppe edge and from the 1820s abolished the khans' power horde by horde. The last great revolt, led by Kenesary Kasymov, was crushed in 1847. The steppe then came under Russian rule, which ended only with the independence of Kazakhstan in 1991.
sum: The Kazakh Khanate was a nomadic state of the Kazakh steppe, east of the Caspian and north of the Aral Sea, from about 1465 until the Russian Empire absorbed it in the first half of the 19th century.
